**Short answer:** Tracing records what your application did, evaluations measure it against curated test cases, and Signals score the traced agent activity in production. The docs I read don't state this three-way relationship in one place, so the sequencing below is my interpretation of how the separate pages connect.

**Roles**
- **Tracing** captures activity. For agents, the Weave SDK models conversations, turns, LLM calls and tool executions, and shows them in the **Agents** tab [S2]. Every turn, LLM call and tool call emits an OpenTelemetry span [S2]. For individual `@weave.op` functions, see the separate Ops/Calls tracing page [S2].
- **Evaluations** are a structured, repeatable measurement. An `Evaluation` object defines a dataset of test examples and scoring functions. Calling `.evaluate()` on it runs it against a model or function and triggers an evaluation run [S3][S8].
- **Signals** score agent turns, applying tags (such as `user-frustration` or `nsfw`) or 0–1 ratings, and show them in the Agents view's Signals tab [S1][S6][S7].

**How they connect**
1. **Trace first.** Signals work on agent turns, so you need traced conversations in the Agents view [S1][S2].
2. **Signals run on that trace data.** You create a signal, and after that Weave scores matching turns [S11]. For a custom signal, you write a definition prompt that Weave sends to an LLM judge. You can also filter which turns are scored and set a sample rate [S11]. The output is tags or ratings on spans [S6].
3. **Signal activity is itself visible in traces.** It appears under **Traces**, which helps you debug scorer errors [S10].
4. **Evaluations are a separate, dataset-driven run.** Their input is your curated examples plus scorers. Their output is an evaluation run whose results you inspect in the UI [S3]. They measure behavior against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and find regressions [S3]. Signals instead monitor production behavior [S1].

**Practical reading:** Use evaluations to measure changes on test cases. Use tracing to record real behavior. Use Signals to flag problems in that traced behavior. I didn't find documentation that feeds signal results automatically into evaluations.

# Trace your agents

> Use the Weave SDK to instrument multi-turn agentic applications and view them in the Agents tab.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tracing/instrument.md).

Learn how to instrument a multi-turn agentic application using the W\&B Weave SDK so that you can view, debug, and evaluate your agent's behavior. This guide is intended for developers who build or integrate agents and want structured visibility into conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool executions.

The Weave SDK for Agents models the full lifecycle of a multi-turn agent conversation: the agent that owns many conversations, the conversation that groups turns together, each user-agent exchange (turn), the LLM calls within a turn, and the tool executions that an LLM triggers. Traces appear in the **Agents** tab of your Weave project. Each conversation shows a multi-turn timeline with nested tool calls, token usage, and feedback.

Weave is built on [OpenTelemetry (OTel)](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/), the open standard for distributed tracing. Every turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OTel *span* (a structured record of one operation). Each span is tagged with [GenAI semantic-convention](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) attributes like `gen_ai.agent.name` and `gen_ai.conversation.id`.

If you're tracing individual functions as Ops with the `@weave.op` decorator, see [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) instead.

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

## Run the evaluation

With your `Evaluation` object, dataset, scorers, and model defined, you're ready to execute the evaluation and capture results in Weave. To run an evaluation, call `.evaluate()` on the `Evaluation` object.

**Python**

Assuming an `Evaluation` object called `evaluation` and a `Model` object to evaluate called `model`, the following code instantiates an evaluation run:

```python lines theme={"system"}
asyncio.run(evaluation.evaluate(model))
```

# Monitor your agents with signals

> Use Weave signals to score agent turns, apply tags, and surface quality and safety issues in production.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tags/create-tag.md).

In Weave's [Agents view](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-activity.md), the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals surface quality and safety issues to flag problems, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need your attention. Use signals to automatically score the quality of your agent's responses, notice when a user is frustrated, or flag NSFW content.

To score turns with an HTTP endpoint that you host instead of an LLM judge, see [Score agent turns with a remote scorer](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/remote-scorer-signals.md).

sources.text:
## Create a custom tag signal

To create a custom tag signal:

1. Navigate to [Forge](https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb) and select your project.

2. In the **Weave project sidebar**, click **Agents**.

3. In the tab bar, click **Signals**.

4. On the Signals tab, click **+ Create your first signal**, or **New signal**.

5. In the drawer, click **Custom Signal**.

   ![The Custom tags drawer with Tag name, Definition, Scorer name, and Inference model fields for creating a custom signal.](https://mintcdn.com/coreweave-dbfa0e8d/3Dv_sw2eg8feUJlx/products/wandb/weave/_media/custom-signal.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=3Dv_sw2eg8feUJlx\&q=85\&s=b01a4b83a0ef2c7717d78efc406a1de0)

6. In the **Custom tags** drawer, configure the following fields:
   * **Tag name**: The label that appears in the Agents view for the behavior you want to monitor.
   * **Definition**: A prompt that describes the behavior you want the signal to detect. Weave sends this prompt to an LLM judge, which scores each agent turn and applies the tag when the turn matches the behavior. For example, to catch a specific product failure: "The user is discussing errors or issues regarding Product X."
   * **+ Add tag** (Optional): Click to define another tag on the same signal. For example, if you support multiple products, add a separate tag for each product so you can track frustration per product instead of only in aggregate.
   * **Scorer name**: The name for the underlying scorer object.
   * **Inference model or custom runtime**: The model used to score matching turns. [Serverless Inference](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/inference/serverless.md) is the default. CoreWeave Serverless Inference consumes credits from your CoreWeave Forge account.
   * **Include tool calls** (Optional): Expand **Advanced**, then check the box to include the turn's tool calls in the context sent to the scoring model.
   * **Only score turns matching** (Optional): Expand **Advanced**, then add one or more filters to restrict which turns the signal scores, for example by agent, operation, tool, or model. Leave empty to score every agent turn. Weave combines multiple filters with `AND` logic.
   * **Sample rate** (Optional): Expand **Advanced**, then set the fraction of matching agent turns the signal scores. For high-traffic agents, lower the sample rate to score a fraction of matching turns instead of every turn and reduce cost.

7. In the **Custom tags** drawer, click **Create signal**.

After you create the signal, Weave scores matching turns. The tag appears in the Agents view, including on the Signals tab.

# Trace your agents

> Use the Weave SDK to instrument multi-turn agentic applications and view them in the Agents tab.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tracing/instrument.md).

Learn how to instrument a multi-turn agentic application using the W\&B Weave SDK so that you can view, debug, and evaluate your agent's behavior. This guide is intended for developers who build or integrate agents and want structured visibility into conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool executions.

The Weave SDK for Agents models the full lifecycle of a multi-turn agent conversation: the agent that owns many conversations, the conversation that groups turns together, each user-agent exchange (turn), the LLM calls within a turn, and the tool executions that an LLM triggers. Traces appear in the **Agents** tab of your Weave project. Each conversation shows a multi-turn timeline with nested tool calls, token usage, and feedback.

Weave is built on [OpenTelemetry (OTel)](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/), the open standard for distributed tracing. Every turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OTel *span* (a structured record of one operation). Each span is tagged with [GenAI semantic-convention](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) attributes like `gen_ai.agent.name` and `gen_ai.conversation.id`.

If you're tracing individual functions as Ops with the `@weave.op` decorator, see [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) instead.

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

## Create a custom tag signal

To create a custom tag signal:

1. Navigate to [Forge](https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb) and select your project.

2. In the **Weave project sidebar**, click **Agents**.

3. In the tab bar, click **Signals**.

4. On the Signals tab, click **+ Create your first signal**, or **New signal**.

5. In the drawer, click **Custom Signal**.

   ![The Custom tags drawer with Tag name, Definition, Scorer name, and Inference model fields for creating a custom signal.](https://mintcdn.com/coreweave-dbfa0e8d/3Dv_sw2eg8feUJlx/products/wandb/weave/_media/custom-signal.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=3Dv_sw2eg8feUJlx\&q=85\&s=b01a4b83a0ef2c7717d78efc406a1de0)

6. In the **Custom tags** drawer, configure the following fields:
   * **Tag name**: The label that appears in the Agents view for the behavior you want to monitor.
   * **Definition**: A prompt that describes the behavior you want the signal to detect. Weave sends this prompt to an LLM judge, which scores each agent turn and applies the tag when the turn matches the behavior. For example, to catch a specific product failure: "The user is discussing errors or issues regarding Product X."
   * **+ Add tag** (Optional): Click to define another tag on the same signal. For example, if you support multiple products, add a separate tag for each product so you can track frustration per product instead of only in aggregate.
   * **Scorer name**: The name for the underlying scorer object.
   * **Inference model or custom runtime**: The model used to score matching turns. [Serverless Inference](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/inference/serverless.md) is the default. CoreWeave Serverless Inference consumes credits from your CoreWeave Forge account.
   * **Include tool calls** (Optional): Expand **Advanced**, then check the box to include the turn's tool calls in the context sent to the scoring model.
   * **Only score turns matching** (Optional): Expand **Advanced**, then add one or more filters to restrict which turns the signal scores, for example by agent, operation, tool, or model. Leave empty to score every agent turn. Weave combines multiple filters with `AND` logic.
   * **Sample rate** (Optional): Expand **Advanced**, then set the fraction of matching agent turns the signal scores. For high-traffic agents, lower the sample rate to score a fraction of matching turns instead of every turn and reduce cost.

7. In the **Custom tags** drawer, click **Create signal**.

After you create the signal, Weave scores matching turns. The tag appears in the Agents view, including on the Signals tab.

After you run an agent with the exporter enabled, Koog forwards traces to your Weave project. Koog's Weave exporter captures the same spans as Koog's general OTEL integration, including:

# Trace your agents

> Use the Weave SDK to instrument multi-turn agentic applications and view them in the Agents tab.

> [!TIP]
>

It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tracing/instrument.md).

Learn how to instrument a multi-turn agentic application using the W\&B Weave SDK so that you can view, debug, and evaluate your agent's behavior. This guide is intended for developers who build or integrate agents and want structured visibility into conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool executions.

The Weave SDK for Agents models the full lifecycle of a multi-turn agent conversation: the agent that owns many conversations, the conversation that groups turns together, each user-agent exchange (turn), the LLM calls within a turn, and the tool executions that an LLM triggers. Traces appear in the **Agents** tab of your Weave project. Each conversation shows a multi-turn timeline with nested tool calls, token usage, and feedback.

Weave is built on [OpenTelemetry (OTel)](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/), the open standard for distributed tracing. Every turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OTel *span* (a structured record of one operation). Each span is tagged with [GenAI semantic-convention](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) attributes like `gen_ai.agent.name` and `gen_ai.conversation.id`.

If you're tracing individual functions as Ops with the `@weave.op` decorator, see [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) instead.

## Create a custom tag signal

To create a custom tag signal:

1. Navigate to [Forge](https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb) and select your project.

2. In the **Weave project sidebar**, click **Agents**.

3. In the tab bar, click **Signals**.

4. On the Signals tab, click **+ Create your first signal**, or **New signal**.

5. In the drawer, click **Custom Signal**.

   ![The Custom tags drawer with Tag name, Definition, Scorer name, and Inference model fields for creating a custom signal.](https://mintcdn.com/coreweave-dbfa0e8d/3Dv_sw2eg8feUJlx/products/wandb/weave/_media/custom-signal.png?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=3Dv_sw2eg8feUJlx\&q=85\&s=b01a4b83a0ef2c7717d78efc406a1de0)

6. In the **Custom tags** drawer, configure the following fields:
   * **Tag name**: The label that appears in the Agents view for the behavior you want to monitor.
   * **Definition**: A prompt that describes the behavior you want the signal to detect. Weave sends this prompt to an LLM judge, which scores each agent turn and applies the tag when the turn matches the behavior. For example, to catch a specific product failure: "The user is discussing errors or issues regarding Product X."
   * **+ Add tag** (Optional): Click to define another tag on the same signal. For example, if you support multiple products, add a separate tag for each product so you can track frustration per product instead of only in aggregate.
   * **Scorer name**: The name for the underlying scorer object.
   * **Inference model or custom runtime**: The model used to score matching turns. [Serverless Inference](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/inference/serverless.md) is the default. CoreWeave Serverless Inference consumes credits from your CoreWeave Forge account.
   * **Include tool calls** (Optional): Expand **Advanced**, then check the box to include the turn's tool calls in the context sent to the scoring model.
   * **Only score turns matching** (Optional): Expand **Advanced**, then add one or more filters to restrict which turns the signal scores, for example by agent, operation, tool, or model. Leave empty to score every agent turn. Weave combines multiple filters with `AND` logic.
   * **Sample rate** (Optional): Expand **Advanced**, then set the fraction of matching agent turns the signal scores. For high-traffic agents, lower the sample rate to score a fraction of matching turns instead of every turn and reduce cost.

7. In the **Custom tags** drawer, click **Create signal**.

After you create the signal, Weave scores matching turns. The tag appears in the Agents view, including on the Signals tab.

**Short answer:** Tracing records what your application did, evaluations measure it against curated test cases, and Signals score the traced agent activity in production. The docs I read don't state this three-way relationship in one place, so the sequencing below is my interpretation of how the separate pages connect.

**Roles**
- **Tracing** captures activity. For agents, the Weave SDK models conversations, turns, LLM calls and tool executions, and shows them in the **Agents** tab [S2]. Every turn, LLM call and tool call emits an OpenTelemetry span [S2]. For individual `@weave.op` functions, see the separate Ops/Calls tracing page [S2].
- **Evaluations** are a structured, repeatable measurement. An `Evaluation` object defines a dataset of test examples and scoring functions. Calling `.evaluate()` on it runs it against a model or function and triggers an evaluation run [S3][S8].
- **Signals** score agent turns, applying tags (such as `user-frustration` or `nsfw`) or 0–1 ratings, and show them in the Agents view's Signals tab [S1][S6][S7].

**How they connect**
1. **Trace first.** Signals work on agent turns, so you need traced conversations in the Agents view [S1][S2].
2. **Signals run on that trace data.** You create a signal (a preset or a custom one with an LLM-judge definition). After creation, Weave scores matching turns. You can filter which turns are scored and set a sample rate [S9]. The output is tags or ratings on spans [S6].
3. **Signal activity is itself visible in traces.** It appears under **Traces**, which helps you debug scorer errors [S10].
4. **Evaluations are a separate, dataset-driven run.** Their input is your curated examples plus scorers. Their output is an evaluation run whose results you inspect in the UI [S3]. They compare changes over time and find regressions [S3]. Signals instead monitor production behavior [S1].

**Practical reading:** Use evaluations to test changes before release. Use tracing to record real behavior. Use Signals to flag problems in that traced behavior. I didn't find documentation that feeds signal results automatically into evaluations.

input.answer:
**Short answer:** Tracing records what your application did, evaluations measure it against curated test cases, and Signals score the traced agent activity in production. The docs I read don't state this three-way relationship in one place, so the sequencing below is my interpretation of how the separate pages connect.

**Roles**
- **Tracing** captures activity. For agents, the Weave SDK models conversations, turns, LLM calls and tool executions, and shows them in the **Agents** tab [S2]. Every turn, LLM call and tool call emits an OpenTelemetry span [S2]. For individual `@weave.op` functions, see the separate Ops/Calls tracing page [S2].
- **Evaluations** are a structured, repeatable measurement. An `Evaluation` object defines a dataset of test examples and scoring functions. Calling `.evaluate()` on it runs it against a model or function and triggers an evaluation run [S3][S8].
- **Signals** score agent turns, applying tags (such as `user-frustration` or `nsfw`) or 0–1 ratings, and show them in the Agents view's Signals tab [S1][S6][S7].

**How they connect**
1. **Trace first.** Signals work on agent turns, so you need traced conversations in the Agents view [S1][S2].
2. **Signals run on that trace data.** You create a signal, and after that Weave scores matching turns [S11]. For a custom signal, you write a definition prompt that Weave sends to an LLM judge. You can also filter which turns are scored and set a sample rate [S11]. The output is tags or ratings on spans [S6].
3. **Signal activity is itself visible in traces.** It appears under **Traces**, which helps you debug scorer errors [S10].
4. **Evaluations are a separate, dataset-driven run.** Their input is your curated examples plus scorers. Their output is an evaluation run whose results you inspect in the UI [S3]. They measure behavior against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and find regressions [S3]. Signals instead monitor production behavior [S1].

**Practical reading:** Use evaluations to measure changes on test cases. Use tracing to record real behavior. Use Signals to flag problems in that traced behavior. I didn't find documentation that feeds signal results automatically into evaluations.
